lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you met the police and the courts. How is criminal law different from civil law? (Criminal law is about crimes; civil law is about disagreements between people.) Today: ages, rights and duties in law.
Laws set ages for many things, to protect young people while they grow and learn. The ages differ between countries, and even within the UK. This unit uses England's as examples.
In England: at 10 you can be held responsible for a crime. At 13 you can do light part-time work. At 16 you can leave school (then study or train to 18) and buy a pet. At 17 you can learn to drive.

At 18 you can vote in a general election and serve on a jury. You can also get a tattoo, buy a lottery ticket and buy alcohol. In Scotland the age of criminal responsibility is 12, and 16-year-olds can vote in Scottish elections.

Other countries choose differently. In many US states teenagers can learn to drive at 15 or 16; in much of Europe, at 17 or 18. The age of criminal responsibility is 12 in Canada and 14 in Germany and Japan. Austria lets 16-year-olds vote.

The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) gives young people rights: safety, education, privacy, being heard, play. If the police stop you, you can ask why. A young suspect in the UK must have an adult there when questioned.

Rights come with responsibilities: obeying the law, respecting other people's rights, and telling the truth in court. Young people who break the law usually go to a youth court, which aims to help them change, not only to punish.
Try it in the world: make an age line in your village from 10 to 18, with a sign at each age saying what England's law allows. Add a second line for another country. Next: fairness for all.

exercises.prompt: In England, how old must you be to vote in a general election?
exercises.hint: Look at the end of the age line.
exercises.explain: You must be 18 to vote in a UK general election.

exercises.prompt: Who sets ages in law, such as for driving or voting?
exercises.explain: Each country's lawmakers set the ages, which is why they differ.

exercises.prompt: The age of criminal responsibility is the same in every country.
exercises.hint: Compare England, Scotland and Germany on the table.
exercises.explain: False: it is 10 in England, 12 in Scotland, 14 in Germany.

exercises.prompt: Which right is in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child?
exercises.explain: The right to be heard on decisions that affect you, with rights to safety, education, privacy and play.

exercises.prompt: Sort these, in England: allowed at 16, or only at 18?
exercises.hint: Remember the marks on the lesson's age line.
exercises.explain: At 16: buy a pet, leave school (then train), ride a moped. At 18: vote, jury service, a tattoo.

exercises.prompt: A person can be held responsible for a crime at 10 in England and at 14 in Germany. How many years' difference is that?
exercises.hint: Take the smaller age from the bigger one.

exercises.prompt: Match each place to its age of criminal responsibility.
exercises.hint: England and Wales is youngest; Japan, like Germany, is oldest of these.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order of the age at which England allows them, youngest first.
items: be held responsible for a crime
exercises.explain: Responsible for a crime 10, light work 13, a pet 16, driving 17, a jury 18.

exercises.prompt: Who must be with a young suspect when the police in the UK question them?
exercises.hint: Someone grown-up who looks after the young person's interests.
exercises.explain: An appropriate adult, such as a parent or a trained volunteer, must be there.

exercises.prompt: Youth courts aim to help young people change, not only to punish.
exercises.hint: Look back at the card about responsibilities.
exercises.explain: True: they try to stop young people offending again.

exercises.prompt: Why do laws set different ages for different things?
choices: each needs different maturity and carries risks
exercises.hint: Compare buying a pet with driving a car.
exercises.explain: Each activity needs a different level of maturity and carries different risks, so the law sets different ages.

exercises.prompt: In England, a 13-year-old may do light work for at most 2 hours on a school day. How many hours is that over 5 school days?
exercises.hint: Multiply the hours a day by the days.

exercises.prompt: Which responsibility goes with the right to be safe?
exercises.hint: Rights belong to everyone, so think about others too.
exercises.explain: Respecting other people's safety: everyone has the same right.

exercises.prompt: Sort these: a right of a young person, or a responsibility?
items: to know why the police stopped you
to tell the truth in court
exercises.hint: A right is owed to you; a responsibility is owed by you.
exercises.explain: Rights: to know why you were stopped, privacy, play. Responsibilities: obey the law, respect others, tell the truth.

exercises.prompt: What is legal for a 16-year-old in one country may not be legal in another.
exercises.hint: Think of driving and voting ages around the world.
exercises.explain: True: each country sets its own ages.
